session.question: How do the sustainability ideas in the supply chain management framework and the article on sustainable marketing both show how environmental sustainability can be advanced and linked to company image?
session.answer:
Both sources present environmental sustainability as a strategic, organization-wide approach rather than a narrow operational add-on. The supply chain management framework shows how ports can advance sustainability by integrating environmental, economic, and social dimensions, aligning actions with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and using the “dashboard of 5 Ps” to guide internal and external collaboration across the supply chain. In this model, sustainability is embedded in governance, planning, and stakeholder coordination, which helps ports contribute to long-term sustainable development. (alamoush2021portsupplychain chunk 1, bratt2021implementingstrategicsustainable chunk 1, mesa2021managementstrategiesand chunk 1)

The sustainable marketing article shows a complementary mechanism: firms can advance environmental sustainability through eco-friendly and socially responsible practices that are communicated to consumers. Sustainable marketing improves brand identity, reputation, customer trust, loyalty, and competitive advantage, thereby linking environmental action directly to company image. In this view, sustainability is both a substantive practice and a reputational asset that differentiates the firm and supports long-term success. (sujanska2023sustainablemarketingand chunk 1)

Together, the two texts show that environmental sustainability can be advanced through integrated management across supply chains and through market-facing communication of responsible practices. In both cases, sustainability strengthens company image by signaling responsibility, credibility, and alignment with broader societal goals. (alamoush2021portsupplychain chunk 1, sujanska2023sustainablemarketingand chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-201a3d29: The article explains that sustainability is increasingly important to a company’s image because consumers want businesses to reduce environmental impact and act responsibly toward society. It argues that adopting sustainable practices and sustainable marketing can improve brand identity, reputation, customer trust, loyalty, and competitive advantage. The study suggests that companies using eco-friendly and socially responsible practices are more likely to attract customers and strengthen long-term success. This supports the idea that sustainability is not only an operational concern but also a strategic tool for shaping positive perceptions of the company and differentiating it from competitors.
From Lucia Šujanská and Margaréta Nadányiová. Sustainable marketing and its impact on the image of the company. Marketing and Management of Innovations, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.21272/mmi.2023.2-06, doi:10.21272/mmi.2023.2-06.

pqac-7859fecb: The article argues that sustainability is increasingly central to a company’s image and brand identity. It says consumers are more environmentally conscious and prefer companies that reduce environmental impact and follow sustainable, ethical practices. By adopting sustainable practices, firms can demonstrate responsibility, build customer trust, improve reputation, and strengthen long-term viability. The paper emphasizes that sustainable marketing can enhance brand image, increase customer loyalty, and provide a competitive advantage, helping companies differentiate themselves, attract new customers, and potentially increase profit. This excerpt does not mention a supply chain management framework, but it clearly links environmental sustainability to company image and reputation.
From Lucia Šujanská and Margaréta Nadányiová. Sustainable marketing and its impact on the image of the company. Marketing and Management of Innovations, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.21272/mmi.2023.2-06, doi:10.21272/mmi.2023.2-06.

pqac-32e3b0f8: The excerpt explains that port supply chain management should integrate the three sustainability dimensions—environment, economy, and society—and be aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. The proposed framework uses measures evaluated through the “dashboard of 5 Ps” (Peace, People, Planet, Partnership, Prosperity) to show how ports can contribute to all SDGs, directly or indirectly. It is described as a conceptual tool for ports to integrate economic and social aspects with environmental concerns and to implement the UN 2030 agenda internally and externally while collaborating with supply chains. This suggests sustainability is not only about environmental action but also about organizational strategy and reputation.
From Anas S. Alamoush, Fabio Ballini, and Dimitrios Dalaklis. Port supply chain management framework: contributing to the united nations’ sustainable development goals. Maritime Technology and Research, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.33175/mtr.2021.247076, doi:10.33175/mtr.2021.247076.

pqac-e816e350: The excerpt explains that the paper proposes a strategic sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) implementation model. It argues that sustainability must be anchored in the company’s vision and integrated across all functions, with organizational learning and collaboration with external stakeholders such as suppliers. The paper emphasizes an operational definition of socioecological sustainability and co-created strategic plans to guide ecological and social improvements while handling tradeoffs with economic concerns. This shows environmental sustainability can be advanced through structured, company-wide practices and stakeholder cooperation, supporting a company’s image as a sustainability leader.
From Cecilia Bratt, Robert Sroufe, and Göran Broman. Implementing strategic sustainable supply chain management. Sustainability, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/su13158132, doi:10.3390/su13158132.

pqac-a68ef3de: The article argues for a supply chain strategy framework tailored to agrifood chains, using Spanish horticultural marketing companies as a case study. It finds that sustainability has become a central concept in collaboration with customers, replacing earlier emphasis on quality and health. The study also shows that collaboration within the chain, especially upstream collaboration, can improve profitability and should be expanded to include suppliers of suppliers. This suggests environmental sustainability is not only a management goal but also tied to cooperative relationships and performance, which can support a company’s image as sustainable and responsible.
From Juan Carlos Pérez Mesa, Laura Piedra‐Muñoz, Emilio Galdeano Gómez, and Cynthia Giagnocavo. Management strategies and collaborative relationships for sustainability in the agrifood supply chain. Sustainability, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/su13020749, doi:10.3390/su13020749.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How do the sustainability ideas in the supply chain management framework and the article on sustainable marketing both show how environmental sustainability can be advanced and linked to company image?

Both sources present environmental sustainability as a strategic, organization-wide approach rather than a narrow operational add-on. The supply chain management framework shows how ports can advance sustainability by integrating environmental, economic, and social dimensions, aligning actions with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and using the “dashboard of 5 Ps” to guide internal and external collaboration across the supply chain. In this model, sustainability is embedded in governance, planning, and stakeholder coordination, which helps ports contribute to long-term sustainable development. (alamoush2021portsupplychain chunk 1, bratt2021implementingstrategicsustainable chunk 1, mesa2021managementstrategiesand chunk 1)

The sustainable marketing article shows a complementary mechanism: firms can advance environmental sustainability through eco-friendly and socially responsible practices that are communicated to consumers. Sustainable marketing improves brand identity, reputation, customer trust, loyalty, and competitive advantage, thereby linking environmental action directly to company image. In this view, sustainability is both a substantive practice and a reputational asset that differentiates the firm and supports long-term success. (sujanska2023sustainablemarketingand chunk 1)

Together, the two texts show that environmental sustainability can be advanced through integrated management across supply chains and through market-facing communication of responsible practices. In both cases, sustainability strengthens company image by signaling responsibility, credibility, and alignment with broader societal goals. (alamoush2021portsupplychain chunk 1, sujanska2023sustainablemarketingand chunk 1)
